name: Marsha Blackburn
bio: Tennessee's senior U.S. senator since 2019, Blackburn is the polling frontrunner with broad establishment support and statewide name recognition. Trump-aligned conservative.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Blackburn's governor campaign does not include a specific early childhood education or pre-K expansion proposal. Her education platform centers on school choice expansion, parental rights, and devolving federal education authority to states. A May 26, 2026, business roundtable with the Greater Memphis Chamber documented her discussing childcare as 'critical workforce infrastructure,' though no new gubernatorial childcare policy proposal emerged. A $1 million donation from Pennsylvania school-privatization billionaire Jeff Yass to a pro-Blackburn PAC continues to underscore her alignment with the school-choice movement.
early_childhood_ed.details: At a June 19, 2026, campaign event in Jackson, Tennessee, Blackburn said she wants to lead the state when federal programs including the U.S. Department of Education are devolved back to states, framing it as an opportunity for 'generational changes' on a conservative path. She has not articulated a pre-K or childcare funding proposal as part of her governor's campaign. On June 20, 2026, reporting by the Tennessee Education Report and The Education Report Substack confirmed that Jeff Yass — a Pennsylvania billionaire credited with funding Tennessee's $300 million private school voucher expansion — donated $1 million to the Team Tennessee PAC supporting Blackburn, making him the largest single contributor in the gubernatorial race. Blackburn is described by these outlets as 'a vocal advocate for private school vouchers.' The Greater Memphis Chamber's 2026 Q2 Government Affairs Update (published July 1, 2026) reported that at a May 26 business roundtable, Blackburn discussed 'childcare as critical workforce infrastructure' alongside topics including public safety, cargo security, and economic development. The report described her as addressing 'federal legislation aimed at supporting safer communities, strengthening prosecution tools, expanding after-school programming, addressing cargo theft and supporting childcare as critical workforce infrastructure.' This framing positions childcare as an economic and workforce issue rather than a child development priority, and does not constitute a new gubernatorial early childhood education policy proposal. A July 2, 2026, WKRN Nashville radio interview focused on public safety, economic development, and data centers without new early childhood education specifics.

child_hunger.summary: Blackburn publicly praised Tennessee's SNAP junk-food purchase restrictions and defended the One Big Beautiful Bill's SNAP cuts. A federal judge blocked Tennessee's planned July 31, 2026, SNAP food restrictions. No new gubernatorial campaign statements on child hunger or SNAP were found in the July 1–6, 2026 window beyond her previously documented June 13, 2026, comments.
child_hunger.details: As previously reported, Blackburn on June 13, 2026, told WJHL/News 2 that Tennessee SNAP recipients who lost benefits 'need to get a job' and defended the One Big Beautiful Bill's SNAP provisions. Tennessee's SNAP junk-food restrictions, which Blackburn had praised, were scheduled to begin July 31, 2026, but a federal judge blocked them on June 23, 2026, ruling the USDA had relied on the wrong section of federal law when approving the pilot projects (WSMV, June 23, 2026). Tennessee Lookout reported on June 16, 2026, that approximately 100,000 Tennesseans have lost SNAP food aid since the One Big Beautiful Bill took effect in July 2025, with SNAP enrollment dropping from 696,000 to 597,890. Additional July 1–3 reporting confirmed the June 22 ruling voided the Tennessee SNAP restriction waivers, with the case (Aragon v. Rollins) blocking enforcement in five states. A July 1, 2026, CSPI white paper estimated the One Big Beautiful Bill cut SNAP funding by roughly $187 billion over a decade and documented that nearly half of the 1.67 million people who lost SNAP in 12 reporting states were children. No new Blackburn statements specifically on child hunger or SNAP as governor candidate were found in the July 1–6, 2026 window.

parental_support.summary: Blackburn championed the One Big Beautiful Bill (signed into law), securing a permanently enhanced Child Tax Credit at $2,200 per child, an expanded employer childcare tax credit, and a permanent Paid Family and Medical Leave Tax Credit. In early July 2026, she received a new endorsement from former Congressman Phil Roe, released an Independence Day message emphasizing 'faith, family, freedom,' and a Washington-based PAC (Tennessee Freedom Fund) spent $1 million on ads boosting her candidacy — but no new specific parental-support or family-benefit policy proposals emerged.
parental_support.details: Sen. Blackburn and Sen. Peter Welch (D-VT) celebrated the Senate's unanimous passage of the bipartisan Baby Changing on Board Act, which would require Amtrak trains to install baby changing stations in all accessible restrooms — citing the nearly nine-hour Memphis-to-New Orleans route used by Tennessee families (published June 16, 2026). Separately, the White House announced it would endorse a slate of children's online safety laws backed by Blackburn — including the Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA) — as part of an AI preemption package (Substrate News, June 15, 2026; Punchbowl News, June 22, 2026). Blackburn's previously documented wins in the One Big Beautiful Bill — a permanently enhanced Child Tax Credit at $2,200 per child, an expanded employer childcare tax credit, and a permanent Paid Family and Medical Leave Tax Credit — remain her primary family financial support record. A June 24, 2026, PAC-produced TV ad touted that 'as governor, Blackburn will lower costs for Tennessee families.' In July 2026, former Congressman Phil Roe endorsed Blackburn on June 30/July 1, praising her conservative values and stating she is 'ready to work to make Tennessee the best state for families and for our veterans.' On July 4, Blackburn released a video message saying she is guided by 'faith, family, freedom, hope, and opportunity.' The Tennessee Freedom Fund PAC spent $1 million on ads tying Blackburn to Trump; a July 2 WKRN interview covered public safety and data centers but no new family support policy specifics. A July 2, 2026, NewsChannel 5 Investigates report highlighted her evasiveness on governor's race questions, with no new policy announcements. No new specific parental support policy proposals were identified in the July 1–6, 2026 window.

name: John Rose
bio: Four-term congressman from the Cumberland Plateau leaving his House seat to run. Farmer and small-business owner from Cookeville.
photo_credit: U.S. House Office of the Clerk

early_childhood_ed.summary: No specific position on early childhood education, pre-K, Head Start, or childcare programs has been found in Rose's governor campaign. At a June 22, 2026, Lincoln Day Dinner appearance, Rose stated that 'we have to continue to improve the outcomes for our kids in education in Tennessee,' but offered no pre-K or childcare policy specifics. No new early childhood education statements were found in the July 1–6, 2026 window.
early_childhood_ed.details: Rose's Tennessee True Tour continued through June 2026, with stops in Grainger County (June 15), Blountville/Sullivan County (June 17), Greeneville (June 17–18), and Chattanooga (June 20). At each stop, Rose emphasized school choice, public school quality, and conservative Tennessee values — but no childcare or early childhood education proposals were identified. At the June 20 Lincoln Day Dinner in Chattanooga, Rose stated improving educational outcomes for children is a priority but gave no early childhood-specific details. His campaign website and public statements from this period continue to focus on K-12 school choice, parental rights, and Career and Technical Education. Rose noted at a Greeneville town hall that 89% of Tennessee children attend public schools, including his own two children, and pledged to appoint a Commissioner of Education with public school teaching experience. A July 3, 2026, Knox News video feature on Rose as a gubernatorial candidate contained no early childhood education policy content. No new statements on early childhood education were found in the July 1–6 window.

child_hunger.summary: As a U.S. Representative, Rose voted for and publicly defended the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, calling it a 'historic accomplishment' that would ensure those in need 'can continue to receive the assistance they need.' A June 17, 2026, ProPublica investigation found that at least 776,000 children nationwide — and approximately 100,000 Tennesseans total — lost SNAP benefits after the bill took effect. Rose did not respond to ProPublica's follow-up questions. No new statements on child hunger or SNAP were found in the July 1–6, 2026 window.
child_hunger.details: ProPublica published a major investigation on June 17, 2026, documenting that more than 776,000 children across 12 states are no longer receiving SNAP benefits since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act took effect in July 2025. The report quoted Rose directly from House Agriculture Committee debate: 'Passing the bill would be a historic accomplishment that will ensure those in need can continue to receive the assistance they need.' ProPublica noted that Rose — along with Rep. Glenn Thompson and Rep. Dusty Johnson — 'did not respond to ProPublica's questions about their statements now that many children no longer receive SNAP benefits.' The Tennessee Lookout separately reported on June 16, 2026, that approximately 100,000 Tennesseans have lost SNAP since July 2025. Rose's governor campaign has not issued any statement on these findings or on child food insecurity during the June 14–29 window or the July 1–6 window. A July 3 Knox News article covering Rose and Blackburn focused on PAC spending and China land attacks, with no child hunger content.

parental_support.summary: No specific positions on paid family leave, child tax credit, or childcare affordability have been identified in Rose's governor campaign. His campaign messaging centers on conservative Tennessee values — 'faith, family, and freedom' — and executive leadership experience, without specific family financial support proposals. No new parental support statements were found in the July 1–6, 2026 window.
parental_support.details: During his June 2026 Tennessee True Tour stops, Rose repeatedly framed his campaign around 'faith, family and freedom' and 'Keep Tennessee Tennessee,' emphasizing protection of Tennessee culture from outside influences. At the June 20 Lincoln Day Dinner, Rose criticized Starbucks' DEI policies and said taxpayer incentives should not go to companies whose values are 'out of step with Tennessee values.' He has not proposed specific paid family leave, child tax credit, or childcare cost relief measures as part of his gubernatorial platform. His campaign continues to position him as a CEO-type executive, describing the governor's job as 'CEO of our state.' Wife Chelsea Rose joined him at campaign events, and the campaign uses the tagline 'faith, family and freedom' but has not translated family rhetoric into specific child-benefit policy proposals. In July 2026, former State Senator Mae Beavers endorsed Rose (TriStar Daily, July 2, 2026), and Trump reportedly told members of Congress he thought Rose 'has been good to me' — neither development involved parental support policy specifics. No new parental support policy statements were found in the July 1–6 window.

name: Monty Fritts
bio: East Tennessee state legislator running on a populist conservative platform. Lower profile statewide than Blackburn or Rose.
photo_credit: No headshot found at direct image URL; visit campaign site

early_childhood_ed.summary: No specific position on early childhood education, pre-K, Head Start, or childcare programs has been found in Fritts' governor campaign. His platform continues to center on liberty, limited government, and Second Amendment rights. A July 2, 2026, national profile confirmed his platform makes no early childhood education proposals, instead emphasizing Christian nationalist ideology and extreme social-conservative positions.
early_childhood_ed.details: A June 26, 2026, Chattanooga Times Free Press profile of Fritts describes his campaign platform as centered on 'liberty and less government' with no mention of early childhood education or childcare policy. Fritts appeared at the June 20 Hamilton County Republican Party Lincoln Day Dinner alongside Blackburn and Rose, where he emphasized grassroots support and limited government but offered no education policy specifics beyond general remarks. A separate WDEF report from June 22, 2026, quoted Fritts saying only 'I don't want them to give it to me. I want to earn it,' with no education-specific remarks. Fritts continues to explicitly oppose taxpayer-funded vouchers (Education Freedom Scholarships) as established in his existing platform, but has not addressed early childhood programs during this period. A July 2, 2026, profile in the Friendly Atheist documented Fritts' self-identification as a 'Christian Nationalist' and his extreme social-conservative positions — including proposed bans on non-Christian religions and abortion criminalization — but contained no reference to early childhood education or childcare policy. A July 3 blog analysis noted Blackburn holds a 'comfortable double-digit lead over Monty Fritts and Jim Rose.' No new early childhood education statements were found in the July 1–6 window.

child_hunger.summary: No specific public position on SNAP, child hunger, Summer EBT, or school nutrition programs has been found in Fritts' governor campaign during the June 14–29 or July 1–6, 2026 windows. His platform's emphasis on limiting government spending is unchanged.
child_hunger.details: Fritts' June 2026 campaign coverage — including a June 26 Chattanooga Times Free Press profile and a June 22 WDEF appearance — focused entirely on his polling position, Second Amendment advocacy, and limited-government philosophy. No statements on SNAP cuts, child food insecurity, or nutrition programs were identified. The Tennessee Lookout's June 16, 2026, report that 100,000 Tennesseans have lost SNAP benefits drew no public response from Fritts. His general anti-spending stance would suggest opposition to expanded food assistance programs, but no explicit position on child hunger has been stated on record. The July 2, 2026, Friendly Atheist profile of Fritts covering his Christian nationalist positions made no reference to child hunger or SNAP. No new child hunger statements were found in the July 1–6 window.

parental_support.summary: No specific public position on paid family leave, the child tax credit, or childcare costs has been found in Fritts' governor campaign. His platform continues to center on liberty and less government. A July 2, 2026, national profile documented his extremist social-conservative positions but contained no family financial support policy proposals.
parental_support.details: Fritts' June 2026 campaign coverage consistently shows a platform focused on limited government, Second Amendment rights, and opposition to career politicians. No statements on paid family leave, child tax credits, employer childcare benefits, or childcare affordability were identified in coverage from June 14–29, 2026. At the June 20 Lincoln Day Dinner and June 22 WDEF appearance, Fritts made no family financial support policy proposals. His campaign's Tennessee Firearms Association online poll result of 46.72% (June 17–26) reflects his Second Amendment constituency focus rather than family policy. The July 2, 2026, Friendly Atheist profile described Fritts as trying to 'out-Christian Marsha Blackburn' with extreme positions including proposed religious bans and abortion criminalization, but contained no parental support or family financial policy proposals. No new parental support statements were found in the July 1–6 window.

name: Lauren Pinkston
bio: Independent gubernatorial candidate. Former Lipscomb University professor with a detailed family-economic platform — only candidate proposing redirecting Education Freedom Scholarship funds to early childhood ed and employer on-site daycare.
photo_credit: Direct headshot URL not found; visit campaign site

early_childhood_ed.summary: Pinkston strongly supports redirecting Tennessee's Education Freedom Scholarship (voucher) funding toward early childhood education, calling it the 'fiscally sound' choice. Two former Republican governors endorsed her in a June 18, 2026, Tennessean op-ed specifically citing this policy as a reason for their support. No new early childhood education policy announcements were found in the July 1–6, 2026 window.
early_childhood_ed.details: On June 18, 2026, former Republican Governors Christine Todd Whitman and Kerry Healey published an op-ed in The Tennessean endorsing Pinkston, explicitly citing her early childhood education policy: 'Pinkston supports redirecting those dollars into early childhood education, not because it is a Democratic or Republican idea, but because it is the fiscally sound one. Closing the gap before kindergarten costs far less than trying to close it at every grade level afterward, and it does not require taking a single dollar from Tennessee's public schools.' The op-ed noted that the overwhelming majority of Education Freedom Scholarship vouchers go to families whose children were already enrolled in private schools, disproportionately serving higher-income households. Pinkston's campaign Substack posts in June 2026 focused on a new data center moratorium policy rather than new early childhood education specifics, but her support for businesses offering on-site childcare and redirection of voucher money to pre-K remains unchanged. Tennessee Firefly (updated July 2026) describes Pinkston as a 'Former Lipscomb University professor and Putnam-area math tutor who built a tutoring operation serving hundreds of Tennessee students at no charge' who 'Opposes Education Freedom Scholarship.' No new early childhood education statements were found in the July 1–6 window.

child_hunger.summary: Pinkston explicitly opposes SNAP benefit restrictions, arguing they harm local grocers and raise costs for middle-class families. No new statements specifically on child hunger or SNAP were found in the July 1–6, 2026 window beyond her previously documented positions.
child_hunger.details: Pinkston's existing platform opposes SNAP benefit restrictions and supports exploring removal of the grocery tax. During the July 1–6 window, no new campaign statements specifically addressing child hunger, SNAP cuts, or summer food programs were identified. The broader Tennessee context — with approximately 100,000 Tennesseans losing SNAP benefits (Tennessee Lookout, June 16, 2026), a federal judge blocking Tennessee's junk-food SNAP restrictions (WSMV, June 23, 2026; Lebanon Democrat, July 1, 2026), and Gov. Bill Lee's rejection of $84 million in federal food assistance funding (Action News 5, July 1, 2026) — did not prompt identified new statements from Pinkston. Her June 19, 2026, Substack post focused on a data center moratorium policy. The June 18 Tennessean op-ed by former governors Whitman and Healey mentioned Pinkston's concern for families who 'can afford their lives' but did not specifically address child hunger or SNAP.

parental_support.summary: Pinkston supports restructuring public assistance to eliminate benefit cliffs that penalize working parents and proposes channeling early childhood education funding toward businesses offering on-site childcare. No new parental support policy announcements were identified in the July 1–6, 2026 window.
parental_support.details: The June 18, 2026, Tennessean op-ed by former Republican Governors Whitman and Healey described Pinkston as a candidate who understands 'what it means to work hard, to know your neighbors' names and to understand that the health of a community is measured by whether the people in it can afford their lives and raise their children with dignity.' The op-ed also highlighted Pinkston as uniquely positioned to negotiate with Tennessee's Republican-supermajority legislature on practical issues including family economic stability. Pinkston's June 19 Substack announcement of a data center moratorium is her primary new policy announcement in that period; it addresses community protection and data rights rather than parental support directly. Her existing positions — eliminating benefit cliffs for working parents and supporting on-site childcare tax incentives — remain unchanged. No new parental support policy announcements were identified in the July 1–6 window.

name: Jerri Green
bio: Democratic primary frontrunner running a coalition campaign rooted in West Tennessee. Focused on healthcare, education, and rural-urban balance.
photo_credit: Green for Governor official campaign website

early_childhood_ed.summary: Green supports universal pre-K, a dedicated childcare and early education fund, expanded home visiting programs, and robust special education investment. In early July 2026, Green continued an intensive statewide campaign — visiting Hamblen County (July 1) and Sevierville (July 4–5 area) — described as addressing issues including voucher-driven diversion of public education funding. A July 5 letter to the editor in the Knox News described her as 'a staunch defender of public education' who addressed Tennessee 'coming in at the bottom on all the good lists (worst state for public education funding due to funneling money to private schools through vouchers).' No new specific early childhood education policy proposals beyond her existing platform were identified in the July 1–6 window.
early_childhood_ed.details: Green campaigned in Kingsport on June 28, 2026 (Kingsport Times News), and was featured in a June 17, 2026, Substack video interview discussing redistricting and how a Democratic governor can fix Tennessee legislative maps. In early July, the Citizen Tribune (July 1, 2026) reported Green held a 'Choose Courage' campaign stop in Hamblen County outlining her vision for Tennessee, drawing more than 50 attendees. A Knox News letter to the editor (July 5, 2026) described Green speaking in Sevierville — her 115th town visited during the campaign — addressing issues including public education funding, healthcare, and family affordability. The letter described her as 'a mother of three and a staunch defender of public education' who spoke to 'a packed room of people from both parties who are sick and tired of Tennessee coming in at the top on all the bad lists' and offering 'Day One real, workable plans.' Tennessee Democratic Chair Rachel Campbell, in a June 27, 2026, NewsChannel 5 segment, cited unaffordable daycare as a key issue the Democratic candidates address: 'People can't afford to put their kids in daycare anymore.' Green's pre-existing platform — universal pre-K, a $50 million TANF-funded childcare waitlist clearance, home visiting programs, and special education investment — remains her stated position.

child_hunger.summary: Green explicitly opposes cuts to SNAP and has pledged to use state resources to combat child food insecurity, stating that one in five Tennessee children goes to bed hungry. In early July 2026, an important new development in Green's home base emerged: Memphis-Shelby County Schools partnered with the Mid-South Food Bank on July 1 to distribute groceries to 250+ families — with local officials citing Gov. Bill Lee's rejection of $84 million in federal child food assistance as a key driver of increased summer hunger need. No new Green-specific SNAP statements were found in the July 1–6 window, but the Memphis context intensifies the relevance of her existing anti-hunger platform.
child_hunger.details: No new Green-specific statements on SNAP or child hunger were identified in the July 1–6, 2026 window. However, the Tennessee context has further intensified: a July 1, 2026, Action News 5 report revealed that Memphis-Shelby County Schools partnered with the Mid-South Food Bank to distribute groceries to more than 250 families, with District 3 Ward Member Stephanie Love calling Gov. Bill Lee's rejection of $84 million in federal child food assistance funding 'a tremendous loss for the family and Memphis and all over Tennessee.' This development is directly relevant to Green's constituents, as Shelby County accounts for approximately 21.92% of Tennessee SNAP recipients (128,795 individuals as of April 2026). The federal judge's June 22–23 blocking of Tennessee's SNAP junk-food restrictions (confirmed in multiple July 1 reports) is also directly relevant to Green's Memphis base. Green's July 1 Hamblen County stop and Sevierville appearance did not surface new child hunger policy statements. Her pre-existing pledge to oppose SNAP cuts and use state resources against food insecurity remains her documented position.

parental_support.summary: Green supports expanded paid family and medical leave, affordable childcare, and a Day One commitment to use $50 million in TANF funds to clear Tennessee's childcare waitlist, as well as a free diaper program. In early July 2026, Green continued active statewide campaigning with stops in Hamblen County and Sevierville — described as addressing issues of family affordability and public education — but no new specific parental support policy announcements were found in the July 1–6 window.
parental_support.details: Green's July 2026 campaign activity included a 'Choose Courage' stop in Hamblen County (July 1, Citizen Tribune) and an appearance in Sevierville covered by a Knox News letter to the editor (July 5). At the Sevierville event, a voter described Green as offering 'Day One real, workable plans' and addressing Tennessee's performance 'at the bottom on all the good lists' including public education funding. The letter noted Green is 'a mother of three' and addressed 'issues that truly matter to Tennesseans trying to raise their families, work at jobs that enable them to afford a decent life.' Tennessee Democratic Chair Campbell's June 27, 2026, NewsChannel 5 appearance framed the Democratic slate as addressing daycare unaffordability and 'making it more affordable to live in Tennessee.' No new Green-specific parental support or family leave policy announcements were identified in the July 1–6 window. Her pre-existing platform — expanded paid family and medical leave, affordable childcare, $50 million TANF-funded childcare waitlist clearance, and a free diaper program — remains her documented position.

name: Dr. Carnita Atwater
bio: Memphis community advocate making her second gubernatorial run. Known for community development work in the New Chicago neighborhood.

early_childhood_ed.summary: No specific early childhood education or pre-K policy position has been published or stated on record by Dr. Carnita Atwater as of July 6, 2026. Her campaign themes continue to center on equity and community empowerment.
early_childhood_ed.details: Atwater was listed among the five Democratic gubernatorial candidates in a June 27, 2026, NewsChannel 5 segment by Tennessee Democratic Chair Rachel Campbell, who framed all Democratic candidates as addressing issues including unaffordable daycare. However, no Atwater-specific statements on early childhood education, pre-K, Head Start, or childcare programs were identified in the June 14–29 or July 1–6, 2026 windows. A Tennessee Firearms Association statewide online poll (June 17–26) showed Atwater at 0.21% among all governor candidates, reflecting her limited media presence compared to frontrunners. Tennessee Firefly (updated July 2026) lists Atwater as having 'No detailed public position' on policy topics including early childhood education. Her campaign themes continue to center on equity, community empowerment, and food access in underserved communities.

child_hunger.summary: Atwater has expressed a commitment to addressing food insecurity in underserved communities, specifically proposing 'portable food satellites in every food desert across Tennessee' to ensure no child goes hungry. No new child hunger policy statements were found in the July 1–6, 2026 window.
child_hunger.details: No new Atwater-specific statements on SNAP, child hunger, Summer EBT, or school nutrition were identified in the June 14–29 or July 1–6, 2026 windows. Atwater's previously documented proposal for 'portable food satellites in every food desert across Tennessee' remains her stated child hunger position. The broader Tennessee SNAP context — approximately 100,000 Tennesseans losing SNAP benefits since July 2025, a federal judge blocking Tennessee's junk-food SNAP restrictions on June 22–23, 2026, and Gov. Bill Lee's rejection of $84 million in federal child food assistance funding (Action News 5, July 1, 2026) — did not generate identified new statements from Atwater. The Tennessee Democratic Party platform, as articulated by Chair Campbell on June 27, 2026, frames all Democratic candidates as working to make life more affordable for Tennessee families, but no Atwater-specific child hunger comments were found.

parental_support.summary: No specific positions on paid family leave, child tax credits, or structured childcare cost relief have been published by Dr. Carnita Atwater as of July 6, 2026.
parental_support.details: No Atwater-specific statements on paid family leave, child tax credits, or childcare affordability were identified in the June 14–29 or July 1–6, 2026 windows. Atwater appeared in a Tennessee Firearms Association poll (June 17–26) with 0.21% support and was listed among Democratic candidates in the June 27 NewsChannel 5 segment by Democratic Chair Campbell, who broadly described all Democratic candidates as addressing issues of affordability including daycare costs — but no Atwater-specific policy proposals on these topics were found. Tennessee Firefly (July 2026) notes '$0' in fundraising and 'Unknown' positions across policy categories for Atwater. Her campaign website and public statements continue to focus on community equity and food access rather than structured family financial support programs.
